title: Founder case: Wrigley follows what customers wanted

sources.claim: William Wrigley Jr. moved to Chicago in 1891 selling soap and offered baking powder as a premium; baking powder proved more popular, he switched to it and offered chewing gum as a premium; the gum proved more popular and he turned to selling chewing gum. (Exact years of each switch differ between sources.)

sections.skill: Apply a documented early decision: follow what customers actually choose

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Wrigley first sell in Chicago?

choices.text: Chewing gum from the very start

questions.intro: Documented history (Britannica): William Wrigley Jr. moved to Chicago in 1891 selling soap and offered baking powder as a premium (a free extra). Baking powder proved more popular, so he switched to selling it and offered chewing gum as a premium. The gum proved more popular, and he turned to selling chewing gum. (Exact years of each switch differ between sources.) Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation): watch what customers actually prefer and be willing to change your main product. One success story does not guarantee the same result for another business.

questions.prompt: What did people keep asking for at the bake sale?
questions.intro: At a school bake sale, you might bring cookies but notice everyone asks for the lemonade you brought as an extra. Next time, you bring more lemonade. That is following evidence: what people actually choose matters more than what you planned. The documented Wrigley facts are the switches; the lesson about following evidence is this course's interpretation.
